paragraphs.text: In 2 unrelated children with epileptic encephalopathy, Li et al. (2016) used exome and candidate panel sequencing to identify the same de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the GRIN2D gene, c.1999G-A (V667I). The mutation lies in the M3 transmembrane domain, which is involved in channel gating. Functional studies showed that it was a gain-of-function mutation. It increased glutamate and glycine potency 2-fold, increased channel open probability 6-fold, and reduced receptor sensitivity to endogenous negative modulators such as extracellular protons. It also prolonged the deactivation time course after glutamate removal.

paragraphs.text: In 3 unrelated patients with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, Tsuchida et al. (2018) used whole exome sequencing to identify novel heterozygous missense variants in the GRIN2D gene. All of the altered residues were highly conserved across vertebrates and among the 4 GluN2 subunits. Structural analysis indicated that all 3 variants probably impair GluN2D function, either by affecting intersubunit interaction or by altering channel gating activity.

paragraphs.text: Li et al. (2016) tested whether the mutant NMDARs were sensitive to FDA-approved NMDAR antagonists and then gave oral memantine to both of their patients. Seizure burden and development improved mildly to moderately. The older proband later developed refractory status epilepticus, which showed dramatic electroclinical improvement with ketamine and magnesium. The authors suggested that NMDAR antagonists may be useful as adjuvant epilepsy therapy in individuals with GRIN2D gain-of-function mutations.

paragraphs.text: Li et al. (2016) used exome and candidate panel sequencing to identify a de novo heterozygous c.1999G-A transition in the GRIN2D gene in 2 unrelated children with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-46 (DEE46). The mutation results in a val667-to-ile (V667I) substitution in the M3 transmembrane domain, which is involved in channel gating. Functional studies showed a gain of function: glutamate and glycine potency increased 2-fold, channel open probability increased 6-fold, sensitivity to extracellular protons was reduced, and deactivation after glutamate removal was prolonged. Transfecting cultured neurons with the mutant cDNA caused dendritic swelling and neuronal cell death.
